analysis.one_liner: Requires farm equipment makers to sell owners and independent repair shops the parts, software, and manuals needed to fix their own machines.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2022 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where no action was ever taken; it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern tractors and combines depend on software, so a broken machine often can't be fixed without the maker's proprietary tools, parts, passwords, and manuals. This bill would have required manufacturers of electronics-enabled farm equipment to make documentation, parts, software, and repair tools available to equipment owners and independent repair shops on fair and reasonable terms, with documentation and software tools essentially free. It would also let people bypass digital locks for repair purposes and let the Federal Trade Commission enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers and ranchers who own or lease equipment, and independent repair shops. When a combine goes down during harvest, farmers could get diagnostic codes, repair manuals, software, and parts directly, instead of waiting days for an authorized dealer, and they could choose a local independent mechanic. The bill set pricing at the same cost and terms manufacturers offer their own authorized dealers, and required free documentation and free software repair tools [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to provide owners and independent repair shops the documentation, parts, software, and tools needed to diagnose, maintain, and repair electronics-enabled farm equipment, on terms no worse than those offered to authorized dealers [S2][S3].

Requires documentation to be provided at no charge and software repair tools to be free and usable without internet access or manufacturer authorization, including tools for bypassing security locks on equipment [S3].

Allows circumvention of digital copyright locks for repair, upgrades, interoperability, and security research, and voids the maker's copyright or patent on any repair item it stops making available [S2][S3].
Requires parts to be replaceable without damaging the machine, using a commonly available tool or one the maker must supply on fair terms [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural equipment manufacturers such as tractor and combine makers, which currently control the repair market and dealer service revenue. They would have to share repair documentation, parts, software, and tools with competitors to their service departments, and could lose copyright and patent protection on items they withhold.
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm equipment manufacturers and their dealer networks

drawbacks.text: Safety, emissions, and tampering concerns: opening security locks and allowing modifications could let changes that affect safety systems or emissions compliance, though the bill explicitly bans modifications that disable safety notifications or push equipment out of emissions or safety compliance [S3].

Intellectual property and trade secret exposure: manufacturers argued the requirement to hand over software and documentation could put proprietary designs at risk, even though the bill says it does not require divulging trade secrets beyond what repair requires [S3].

Compliance cost and friction for manufacturers: fair and reasonable terms are defined as matching the best deal given to authorized dealers, which means writing, updating, and policing new repair-supply arrangements, with enforcement by the FTC [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For farmers, the benefit is substantial: repair delays during planting and harvest are expensive, and dealer-only repair can cost far more than an independent job. The main costs fall on manufacturers, whose service revenue and control over their machines would shrink. The bill's carve-outs for safety and emissions rules and trade secrets address the most serious objections, making this a fairly targeted fix rather than a sweeping mandate, though its public-domain penalty for withholding repair items was aggressive by copyright standards.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in February 2022 and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Tester introduced the bill on February 1, 2022, joined by Sen. Martin Heinrich...

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm equipment manufacturers and their dealer networks, which keep exclusive control over parts, software, and repair revenue for electronics-enabled machines.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm equipment manufacturers and their dealers

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, the main push behind it.

against.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill and took no further action; it was never considered by the committee and never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and the bill gained no Republican support in a chamber where it needed committee and floor action to advance.
